title: Converting Between Types
description: Moving a value from one type to another, static_cast, and the whole-number division trap.

content.value: Every whole number is also a decimal: 7 is the same value as 7.0. So an `int` moves into a `double` automatically. This is **widening**: nothing can be lost.

content.caption: The `double` prints as `7` because `cout` drops zeros it does not need. Half of it is 3.5, not 3: it really is a `double`.

content.value: A `double` can hold 7.9, an `int` cannot. Many languages refuse this move. C++ does it **silently**, so a mistake can slip past.

items.title: Silent
items.text: Compiles, but nothing tells the reader that .9 was lost.

content.title: Same result, different message
content.caption: A **cast** names the type you are converting to. It says: I know this loses something, and I mean it.
7.9 became 7, not 8: converting to `int` throws the decimal part away. Old code writes `(int) price`, the C style. This course uses `static_cast`.

content.question: What is `static_cast<int>(-2.7)`?
content.explain: A cast to `int` throws the decimal part away. It never rounds, so -2.7 becomes -2. Real rounding uses `round`, later in the course.

content.value: When both sides of `/` are `int`, C++ does whole-number division: it throws the remainder away before anything else happens.

steps.note: Both sides of the coming division are `int`.
One side is a `double`, so the answer keeps its fraction.
Not a fix: `7 / 2` is worked out as 3 first, then widened to 3.0.
The cast turns 7 into 7.0 before dividing. Fixed in time.
The type on the left could not repair it. `cout` prints 3.0 as `3`.
Casting one side gives the real answer.

content.title: Where the 0.5 goes

content.value: Percentages bite hardest. `correct * 100 / total` loses the fraction. `correct * 100.0 / total` keeps it.

content.value: A `char` is stored as a number code. `'A'` is 65. So a `char` fits in an `int`, and `static_cast<char>` turns a number back into a character.

content.caption: Adding two chars adds their codes: 65 plus 66 is 131.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `'A' + 1` is arithmetic on the code: 65 plus 1. To get the letter B you must cast with `static_cast<char>`.

quiz.question: What does `double d = 7; cout << d << endl;` print?
quiz.explain: Widening an `int` into a `double` is automatic and safe. `cout` then leaves off the `.0` because it adds nothing.

quiz.question: What does `static_cast<int>(7.9)` give?
options: 8, because it rounds to the nearest whole number
7, because it chops the decimal part off
quiz.explain: Converting to `int` throws the fractional part away rather than rounding. For rounding there is a separate tool, `round`.

quiz.question: What does `cout << 7 / 2 << endl;` print?
quiz.explain: Both values are `int`, so C++ does whole-number division and drops the remainder. Making either side a `double` gives 3.5.

quiz.question: Does `double answer = 7 / 2;` store 3.5?
options: Yes: the type on the left makes it a decimal division.
No: the division happens first as ints, so it stores 3.
No: it does not compile at all.
quiz.explain: The right hand side is worked out before anything is stored, so 3 is produced and then widened. Convert one side of the division instead.

quiz.question: How do you turn the text `"42"` into the number 42?
options: You cannot: text can never become a number.
quiz.explain: A cast only works between related types, and text is not a number type. `stoi` parses the characters and works out the value they spell.

quiz.question: What is `static_cast<char>(66)` if `'A'` has code 65?
quiz.explain: Characters are stored as codes, so the code one after `'A'` is `'B'`. Converting an `int` to a `char` looks up the character with that code.
